You hear a discussion between a physician and nurse explaining about schistosomiasis and its causes.
Now, read the question.
Hello, Doctor. What is schistosomiasis and what are its causes?
Schistosomiasis, also termed as bilharzia, is caused by parasitic worms.
Although these worms are not found in the U.S., more than 200 million people are affected
worldwide by this disease. In terms of impact, this disease stands next to malaria as the most
devastating parasitic disease. Schistosomiasis is also considered one of the neglected tropical
diseases. The parasites causing schistosomiasis dwell in certain types of freshwater snails.
The infectious form of the parasite, known as cercariae, emerge from the snail,
therefore contaminating water. Most human infections are caused by Schistosoma mansoni,
S. japonicum, or S. hematobium. One can become infected when the skin is exposed to contaminated
fresh water.
Question 26.
You hear a discussion between two doctors about the importance of measuring serum amylase or serum lipase.
Now read the question.
Doctor, can you explain to me whether measuring serum amylase or serum lipase is significant
for acute pancreatitis?
Well, measuring both serum lipase and serum amylase is not necessary.
Measuring serum lipase alone is adequate for diagnosing acute pancreatitis, since it is
more effective than serum amylase, especially because it rises more quickly and remains
elevated longer. According to a study of 151 patients with acute pancreatitis,
the sensitivity of lipase was about 97% and the specificity was almost 100%.
Contrarily, the sensitivity of amylase was just 79% and the specificity was 99%.
Therefore, amylase should be replaced by lipase as the first line laboratory investigation for suspected acute pancreatitis.
Question 27.
You hear a discussion between two doctors about the misdiagnosing of acute cardiorenal syndrome as renal injury due to hypovolemia.
Now, read the question.
Hello, doctor.
What is your opinion about misdiagnosing of acute cardiorenal syndrome as renal injury
due to hypovolemia?
Often, acute cardiorenal syndrome is misdiagnosed for renal injury due to hypovolemia.
Patients with stable heart failure normally have mild hypervolemia at baseline. However,
they can become hypovolemic due to severe diarrhea, overaggressive diuretic therapy,
or other causes. Although the fluid status of these two conditions are different,
they are often difficult to distinguish. Urine electrolytes suggest a pre-renal acute kidney
injury in both of these conditions. However, a history of recent diuretic overuse or recent
fluid losses may help identify hypovolemia. If available, analyzing of the recent trend in weight
will be essential in making the right diagnosis. Misdiagnosis of acute cardiorenal syndrome as
hypovolemia-induced acute kidney injury will be catastrophic. In case the volume depletion in
acute cardiorenal syndrome is erroneously judged to be the cause of acute renal injury. Therefore,
fluid administration can further worsen both renal and cardiac function.
Question 28. You hear a physician explaining to his nurse about sepsis and infection. Now read the question.
Doctor, what is sepsis?
Sepsis is the extreme response from our body to an infection.
This is a life-threatening condition, and without timely treatment, sepsis can rapidly
cause tissue damage, organ failure, and mortality.
This happens when an individual already has an infection in his lungs, skin, urinary tract,
or somewhere else, triggering a chain reaction throughout the body.
types of infection that are often connected with sepsis are lungs, kidney, skin, and gut,
and the most frequently identified germs that cause infections and can develop into sepsis
include staphylococcus aureus or staph, Escherichia coli, and certain types of streptococcus.
An infection occurs when germs enter into the body and multiply, causing illness, organ and tissue
damage or disease. In case that infection grows aggressively resulting in a life-threatening
condition is called sepsis.
Question 29. You hear a discussion between two doctors about brain imaging prior to lumbar
puncture in the suspected cases of bacterial meningitis. Now, read the question.
Hello, doctor. Can you please explain to me when the brain should start the imaging precede
lumbar puncture in the suspected cases of bacterial meningitis?
For the patients with immunodeficiency or focal neurologic deficits or with altered mental status
or seizures in the past seven days, a brain imaging should be performed prior to lumbar
puncture. Moreover, corticosteroid therapy and empiric antibiotic should be started immediately
after lumbar puncture without waiting for the results. Brain imaging should precede lumbar
puncture in patients with focal neurologic deficits or immunodeficiency, or with altered
mental status or seizures during the previous week. However, lumbar puncture can be safely
done in most patients without first obtaining brain imaging. In case the lumbar puncture is
to be delayed, then these treatments should be started immediately after obtaining the
blood culture report.

Managing Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
Patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage are at high risk of complications such as
delayed cerebral ischemia, re-bleeding, cerebral infarction, and mortality.
The main symptom is the abrupt onset of severe headaches.
When this condition is suspected, a tomography without contrast should be performed.
However, positive outcomes are seen when patients are managed in a high-volume center with a specialized neurointensive care unit.
Early aneurysm repair by surgical clipping or endovascular coiling is the best strategy to reduce the risk of re-bleeding.

Medical and neurologic complications such as increased intracranial pressure, hydrocephalus, seizures, hyponatremia, delayed cerebral ischemia, hypovolemia, and cardiac and pulmonary abnormalities are extremely common.

Cardiac and renal function are intricately interdependent, and failure of either of these
organs causes injury to the other organ in a vicious cycle of worsening function.
We are going to discuss about the acute exacerbation of heart failure or acute cardiorenal syndrome
resulting in acute kidney injury, which is a common cause of admission to the intensive care unit.
Let us examine the clinical definition, pathophysiology, hemodynamic derangements,
clues that help in diagnosing and treatment. Cardio-renal syndromes are a group of
interconnected disorders involving the heart and kidneys, which are classified based on whether
the problem is acute or chronic and whether the primary problem is in the heart, called
cardiorenal syndrome, the kidneys, called renocardiac syndrome, or another organ, called
secondary cardiorenal syndrome. Although the above definitions provide a good general description,
there is a necessity of further clarification of the nature of organ dysfunction.
Acute renal dysfunction can be unambiguously defined using an akin and rifle classification.
Here, akin means acute kidney injury network, and rifle means risk, injury, failure, loss of kidney function, and end-stage kidney disease.
On the other hand, acute cardiac dysfunction is an ambiguous term that include pathophysiologically and clinically distinct conditions.
Acute Heart Failure and Cardiogenic Shock
Cardiogenic shock is characterized by an abrupt compromise in cardiac pump functioning resulting in global hypoperfusion that is severe enough to cause systemic organ damage.
On the other hand, acute heart failure is defined as gradually or rapidly worsening symptoms and signs of congestive heart failure due to worsening pulmonary or systemic congestion.
Hypervolemia is the hallmark of acute heart failure, whereas patients with cardiogenic shock may be hypovolemic or normovolemic.
Although cardiac output may be mildly decreased in certain cases of acute heart failure,
systemic perfusion is adequate to maintain the organ functioning. However, these two conditions
cause renal injury by distinct mechanisms and have entirely different therapeutic implications.
Reduced renal perfusion because of renal venous congestion is now considered as the major
hemodynamic mechanism of renal injury in acute heart failure. On the other hand, in cardiogenic
shock, renal perfusion is reduced due to a critical decrease of cardiac pump function.
Therefore, the ideal definition of acute cardiorenal syndrome should describe a distinct
pathophysiology of the syndrome and provide distinct therapeutic options that can counteract.
Hence, we suggest that renal injury due to cardiogenic shock should not be included in its definition.
So, discussion of acute cardiorenal syndrome is limited to renal injury caused by acute heart failure.
Multiple mechanisms have been implicated in the pathophysiology of cardiorenal syndrome.
Sympathetic hyperactivity is a compensatory mechanism in heart failure
and may be aggravated in case cardiac output is further decreased.
Its effect include constriction of afferent and efferent arterioles,
causing decreased renal perfusion and increased tubular sodium and water reabsorption.
Different strategies can be followed to prevent acute cardiorenal syndrome.
An optimal outpatient diuretic regimen to avoid hypervolemia is very critical.
Patients with advanced congestive heart failure should be monitored thoroughly in dedicated heart failure clinics until their diuretic regimen is optimized.
Patients should be advised to get their weight checked periodically and seek medical opinion if they observe any increase in their weight or a decrease in their urine output.

Hello, doctor.
Can the patients with endocarditis be safely anticoagulated?
Managing anticoagulation in patients with endocarditis needs a personalized approach,
using a careful risk-benefit evaluation on a case-by-case basis. There is a lack of high
quality evidence. Therefore, the recommendations also vary according to the clinical condition.
Newly diagnosed native valve with endocarditis itself is not an indication of anticoagulation.
The question of anticoagulation arises in patients who have a pre-existing or co-existing
indication for anticoagulation, such as deep vein thrombosis, atrial fibrillation,
pulmonary embolism, or an artificial prosthetic heart valve. The question becomes yet more complex
in patients with cerebrovascular complications and a co-existent strong indication for anticoagulation.
Earlier studies have suggested a significant risk of cerebral hemorrhage with anticoagulation
in patients with native valve endocarditis. Consequently, some experts have expressed
skepticism about these findings. Moreover, this skepticism arises from the studies that showed
a lower incidence of cerebrovascular complications and smaller vegetation size in patients with
prosthetic valve with endocarditis, in which most of the patients received anticoagulation therapy.
The mechanism responsible for this effect is considered that the vegetation is an amalgam
of destroyed cells, fibrin, and platelets, with anticoagulation preventing the growth
and propagation of this aggregation. Some experts are of the view that the incidence
of ischemic stroke with hemorrhagic transformation in patients with endocarditis receiving anticoagulation
is overestimated. According to this concept, the beneficial effects at least counterbalance
the harmful effects of anticoagulation. Moreover, the recent studies have shown that
patients on anticoagulation tend to have fewer cerebrovascular complications and smaller
vegetations. The studies reveal that not only are the cerebrovascular complications less common in
patients who were already on anticoagulation when endocarditis was diagnosed, but also there was no
increase in the rate of hemorrhagic lesions. These were all non-randomized studies, and most of the
patients had native valve with endocarditis diagnosed at an early stage. Significantly,
these studies revealed that there were only beneficial effects of anticoagulation if the
patient was receiving warafin before the diagnosis of endocarditis and initiation of antibiotic
therapy. No benefits from anticoagulation were seen once antimicrobial therapy had begun.
Therefore, starting anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy for the sole purpose of
stroke prevention is not advised for the patients with newly diagnosed endocarditis.
For most of the patients with endocarditis and stroke or suspected stroke, anticoagulation
and antiplatelet therapy should be temporarily discontinued.
This is a need of careful evaluation individualized assessment of the patients and the risk
factors predisposing the patients to cerebrovascular complications such as large
vegetations or very mobile vegetations or causative pathogens such as candida SPP or S.
aureus, therefore may prompt temporary suspension of antiplatelet and anticoagulation therapy.
In case there is a clear pre-existing or co-existing indication for these agents
and surgery is not expected, consider continuing anticoagulant and antiplatelet therapy,
providing that patients are free from the risk factors described above and suspicion of stroke
has been excluded. In case surgery is considered for the patients with a clear pre-existing or
coexisting indication for these agents, then a short-acting anticoagulant such as intravenous
or low molecular weight heparin can be given as a bridge to surgery.
